title: Database Indexing — Flashcards
subtitle: 40 cards across 9 categories · Click to flip · Export to Anki / Quizlet

cards.a: A separate data structure that provides a fast path to locate records without scanning every row. Trades extra disk space and slower writes for much faster reads.
The default storage format for table data — rows written in no particular order, like a notebook where entries are added as they come.
Reading every row in a table one by one to find matching records. What happens when no index exists for the query. Very slow on large tables.
Sequential I/O reads data in order from disk — very fast. Random I/O jumps to scattered locations — much slower, even on SSDs.
A self-balancing tree where each node holds sorted keys and pointers. Nodes have many children (hundreds), keeping the tree shallow so any record is found in 2–3 disk reads.
A B-tree variant where all data lives in leaf nodes and internal nodes store only navigation keys. Leaf nodes are linked for efficient sequential scans. Used by MongoDB.

cards.q: Why B-tree nodes match disk page size
cards.a: Each disk read loads exactly one page (typically 8KB). Sizing nodes to one page means each tree traversal step costs exactly one disk read — maximizing I/O efficiency.
Equality searches (=), range queries (>, <, BETWEEN), ORDER BY, and prefix matches (LIKE 'abc%'). The default index for most databases.
Arbitrary substring matches (LIKE '%keyword%'), full-text search, or proximity-based spatial queries. These don't map to the tree's sorted order.
PostgreSQL automatically creates a B-tree index for every PRIMARY KEY and every UNIQUE constraint — no CREATE INDEX statement needed.

A storage architecture optimized for writes. New data goes to an in-memory buffer, gets logged for durability, then is flushed to disk in large sequential chunks. Background compaction keeps files tidy.
The in-memory write buffer in an LSM tree. Writes land here first in a sorted structure. When full, it's flushed to disk as an immutable SSTable.
An immutable sorted file on disk produced when a memtable is flushed. Because the memtable was already sorted, the flush is one fast sequential write.
A sequential append-only log that records every write before it hits the memtable. If the database crashes, the WAL is replayed to recover uncommitted data.
A background process that merges multiple SSTables into larger ones, removing duplicates and deleted entries. Keeps the number of files manageable and improves read speed.

cards.q: LSM trees vs B-trees: the core tradeoff
cards.a: LSM trees: very fast writes (batched, sequential) but slower reads (must check multiple SSTables). B-trees: balanced reads and writes with predictable 2–3 disk reads per lookup.
A probabilistic structure attached to each SSTable. Can definitively say a key is NOT in the file (no false negatives), letting the database skip most SSTables without reading them.
Write-heavy systems: metrics ingestion, logging, IoT data, time-series. When you write far more than you read and can tolerate slightly higher read latency.
A persistent hashmap that maps column values directly to their row locations. Achieves O(1) average lookups for exact-match queries. Useless for range queries or sorting.

cards.q: Hash index vs B-tree: why B-trees usually win
cards.a: B-trees handle equality lookups almost as fast (2–3 disk reads) while also supporting range queries and ORDER BY. Hash indexes are faster in theory but far less flexible.
In-memory databases like Redis where all data is in RAM and the primary use case is exact-match key-value lookups.

cards.q: Why lat/lng B-tree indexes fail for proximity search
cards.a: Proximity is a 2D circular problem. A B-tree on latitude produces a global strip; using both lat and lng produces a rectangle — both much larger than the actual search radius.
Converts 2D coordinates into a 1D string by recursively dividing the world into quadrants. Nearby locations share similar string prefixes, enabling proximity search via B-tree prefix scans.
A tree that recursively divides 2D space into four equal quadrants. Dense areas get subdivided more finely. Foundational concept but rarely used in production today.
The production-standard spatial index. Groups nearby objects into flexible, overlapping bounding rectangles that adapt to actual data. Handles points and shapes in one index.
Two locations physically adjacent but on opposite sides of a geohash cell boundary may have very different prefix strings. Fixed by also searching the 8 neighboring cells.

Geohash: simpler, leverages existing B-tree, great for points. R-tree: more accurate, no boundary artifacts, handles shapes. R-tree is the production standard; geohash is the elegant interview answer.
Maps terms (words) to the list of documents containing them. Like the index at the back of a textbook — look up a word, get all the pages where it appears.
Processes text before indexing: tokenize → lowercase → remove stop words → stem. Allows 'Databases' to match 'database', 'DATABASE', and 'database's'.
Reducing words to their root form during text analysis. 'Running', 'runs', 'ran' all become 'run', so a search for any form matches all of them.
Common words (like 'the', 'and', 'is') removed during text analysis because they appear in almost every document and add no search value.
A single index on multiple columns in a specific order. Internally a B-tree keyed on the concatenation of columns — handles filtering and sorting in one traversal.
A composite index on (A, B, C) can only be used efficiently for queries that include column A. Skipping the leading column means the B-tree's sorted order provides no useful path.
An index that includes all columns a query needs (filter + return columns). The database serves the entire result from the index, skipping the main table lookup entirely.
Faster reads by avoiding table lookups, but larger index size and more write overhead. As of 2026, modern query optimizers often make them unnecessary — use only when you have a clear reason.
Every INSERT or UPDATE must update the main table AND every index on it. A table with 5 indexes triggers 6 writes per insert.

cards.q: When indexes hurt more than help
cards.a: Write-heavy, read-rare tables (like audit logs) — index maintenance overhead outweighs the benefit. Also very small tables where a sequential scan is already fast.
B-tree. Handles equality, ranges, sorting, and prefix matching. Used by default in PostgreSQL, MySQL, and MongoDB. Only exceptions: spatial data → geospatial; full-text → inverted.

cards.q: When to use an inverted index
cards.a: Full-text search — finding keywords anywhere in a document. Used by Elasticsearch, Lucene, and PostgreSQL's tsvector for search features.

cards.q: When to use a geospatial index
cards.a: Proximity searches — finding nearby points given a latitude and longitude. Standard B-tree indexes on lat/lng don't understand 2D spatial relationships.
